The bridge was built in 1954. It was supposed to last fifty years. It lasted seventy-two. Last month, engineers declared it structurally deficient. The city council voted to close it immediately. Fifteen thousand commuters now take a forty-minute detour every day. Businesses on the east side have lost a third of their customers. A replacement will cost three hundred million dollars. The federal government has offered nothing. The state has offered half. The gap remains. This is the infrastructure crisis no one wants to talk about. Bridges. Roads. Water pipes. They are all aging. They are all failing. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave the nation a C-minus. That was generous. Politicians promise fixes every election cycle. The fixes never come. Meanwhile, a city of two hundred thousand people drives an extra hour each day because a bridge that should have been replaced twenty years ago was not.
